narrative: Star Vetter automatically finds candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite and checks them for reliability. When TESS observes a star's brightness over time, eclipsing binaries produce a distinctive pattern: periodic dips as one star passes in front of the other. Our pipeline samples target stars, measures their light curves, applies statistical tests to separate real signals from noise, and cross-checks against six major variable-star catalogs to avoid re-reporting known objects. Candidates that survive these gates undergo a fully automated pixel-level check to confirm the signal comes from the target star itself, not from nearby contaminants. We report 303 confirmed candidates from our sample so far. The process is designed to be conservative: we start with over 20,000 targets but apply multiple vetting stages, each one filtering out false positives. Because each candidate has passed both statistical rigor and automated pixel verification, the results are trustworthy for further study, though individual candidates may carry caveats noted on their pages.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other in such a way that, from Earth's viewpoint, one star periodically passes in front of the other. When this happens, the total brightness of the system dips. These dips repeat at regular intervals equal to the orbital period. TESS can detect these brightness changes, even for distant or faint systems.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a 'candidate' and a 'confirmed' candidate on this site?
faqs.answer: A candidate is any star that shows a signal consistent with an eclipsing binary after statistical vetting and novelty checking. A confirmed candidate is one that has passed the automated pixel-level check, which verifies that the signal comes from the target star itself rather than from a nearby background star or other source of contamination. All candidates listed on this site are confirmed in that sense.

faqs.question: What is the ML screening score and what does it do?
faqs.answer: Star Vetter includes a machine learning model trained on 3,092 labeled examples to assess candidate quality. It outperforms our baseline statistical rule set. However, the ML score is a second opinion only and does not currently gate or filter which candidates receive the pixel-level check. All candidates that pass statistical vetting go to pixel check regardless of the ML score.

faqs.question: How is each candidate checked?
faqs.answer: Every candidate undergoes a fully automated pixel-level check. This process examines the light curve at the pixel level to confirm that the eclipse signal originates from the target star and not from nearby stars or instrumental artifacts. The check is performed automatically by software, not by visual inspection or human review.

faqs.question: What happens if the orbital period looks like it could be aliased?
faqs.answer: We perform an odd/even eclipse-depth test: we compare the depth of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses. If these depths differ significantly, the true orbital period may be twice what the light curve initially suggests. Candidates with strong indications of period aliasing are flagged, and this information is available on their individual pages.

faqs.question: Can I verify a candidate myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each confirmed candidate includes links to its TESS light curve data and orbital parameters (period and eclipse depths) measured from the data. You can access the raw time-series photometry and examine the signal yourself using public TESS archives and analysis tools.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it's listed here?
faqs.answer: Listing on Star Vetter is the end of this pipeline's workflow. The project does not conduct follow-up observations, perform spectroscopy, submit results to scientific journals, or maintain contact with external research groups. Each candidate's page includes all results from our automated checks; further study or confirmation is the responsibility of other researchers.

faqs.question: How much of the sky has this project covered?
faqs.answer: Star Vetter has sampled about 2.4% of the target stars available in TESS data so far. This means the current results represent a portion of the full survey potential, and many more candidates may be found as processing continues.
